To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
students’ writing trajectories were shaped by the interplay between vocational and academic discourses, and that this interplay was mediated by the students’ “professional habitus”.
the students’ writing trajectories are characterized by a tension between academic and vocational writing practices.
the students’ writing trajectories are shaped by academic discourse and “professional habitus”.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways that the students are positioned in relation to the academic field, and how they position themselves as future professionals.
how students in ECEC are positioned in the transition between the academic and the vocational field.
the question of how students in teacher education develop their writing skills in relation to academic and vocational discourse.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the writing trajectories in the student thesis can be described as “professional habitus” (Bourdieu 1998) in a process of academisation.

students are not necessarily “resisting” or “opposing” academic writing, but rather “negotiating”, and that they are not necessarily “opposing” the academic writing, but “negotiating” it, and that they are negotiating the academic writing in the context of their own professional habitus.

the students’ writing trajectories can be described as an ongoing process of negotiation between academic discourses and “professional habitus”, which can be seen as an expression of the vocational field.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
students’ academic writing trajectories are shaped by a professional habitus, a set of values and practices that is shared by students and teachers, and which is also reflected in their writing.
the student writing trajectory in ECEC is shaped by a vocational habitus, which is in the process of being reconfigured by an emerging academic habitus.

the students’ writing trajectories are shaped by the academic field, the vocational field, and the students’ “professional habitus”, which is the students’ own understanding of what is relevant to write about in a student thesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

students’ writing is shaped by the vocational field and its “professional habitus”, and not primarily by the university’s academic culture and its “intellectual habitus”, and that this is a matter of concern.
the students’ professional habitus, shaped by their professional field, is a key factor in their writing trajectories.
students’ writing trajectories are not only influenced by the academic discourses they are exposed to, but also by their vocational “habitus” and the professional field they are about to enter.
